content.title: What are LinkedList and Queue?
content.description: LinkedList is a doubly linked list implementation of both the List and Deque interfaces, while Queue is an interface designed to process elements in a specific order, usually FIFO (First-In, First-Out).

content.content: Unlike ArrayList, which stores elements in a dynamic array, LinkedList stores elements as interconnected nodes. This makes insertions and deletions more efficient. Since LinkedList also implements the Queue interface, it can be used for queue operations such as adding and removing elements in FIFO order.

content.title: Why Learn LinkedList & Queue?
content.content: LinkedList is ideal for frequent insertions and deletions, while Queue is widely used for scheduling, task processing, BFS traversal, and message handling.
A LinkedList stores elements as nodes where each node contains data and references to the previous and next nodes. It maintains insertion order and allows duplicate elements.

content.title: Where are LinkedList and Queue Used?

items.question: CPU Scheduling
items.answer: Tasks are processed in queue order.

items.question: Breadth-First Search (BFS)
items.answer: Queues store vertices to visit next.

items.question: Print Queue
items.answer: Documents are printed in FIFO order.

items.question: Music Playlist
items.answer: LinkedList allows efficient insertion and deletion of songs.

content.title: People Waiting in Line
content.content: A queue works like people standing in a ticket line. The first person to join the queue is the first one to be served. A LinkedList is like a chain where every person knows who stands before and after them.

content.title: Interview Importance
content.content: Interview questions commonly cover LinkedList vs ArrayList, Queue operations, FIFO behavior, internal node structure, and the time complexity of insertion, deletion, and traversal.

items.question: Is LinkedList always faster than ArrayList?
items.answer: No. LinkedList is faster for insertions and deletions, while ArrayList is faster for random access.

items.question: Does Queue allow direct index access?
items.answer: No. Queue elements are accessed according to processing order.

items.question: Should remove() be used on an empty queue?
items.answer: No. Use poll() when possible because it returns null instead of throwing an exception.

content.title: Remember This
content.description: Use LinkedList when insertions and deletions are frequent, and use Queue when data must be processed in FIFO order.
